overview.lead: How do cities make SDG 11 a reality? This dashboard explores pioneering urban projects across Europe – and shows what it takes to replicate them. Every highlighted city runs a flagship project that addresses the SDG's Subgoals. Each project is backed by measurable data and traceable sources. You can explore the full project story (Problem Fit), what it achieved (Impact), and how to adopt it (Adoption Requirements).

adoption.info.politics: A decisive factor in the project’s success was the close cooperation between the city administration and the public. The citizens’ initiative #RingFrei played a key role: it set out a ten-point plan and kept up steady pressure on city politics. The City of Cologne worked closely with that alliance.
adoption.koeln.politics.rec.movement.tit: A citizens’ movement as the engine
adoption.koeln.politics.rec.movement.cla: The project is a prime example of how an engaged civil society can shape and drive a political process.
adoption.koeln.politics.rec.movement.exa: What Cologne did: #RingFrei was not a loose alliance but a strategically organised citizens’ movement with a clear ten-point plan. It sustained political pressure over years — through media presence, public actions and a persistent watch on what the administration was doing. That stamina, and the concreteness of its demands, is what stopped them fading away and got them implemented step by step.
adoption.koeln.politics.rec.movement.les: The lesson: a strong, organised citizens’ movement is often the decisive catalyst for political change in transport policy. Administrations respond more readily to concrete, well-argued demands from a broad alliance than to isolated voices. The ideal is professional planning inside the administration paired with an active civil society that formulates demands, offers alternatives and follows the delivery critically.
adoption.koeln.politics.rec.phased.title: Deliver it in stages
adoption.koeln.politics.rec.phased.claim: Cologne did not do it all at once, but worked through a phased process over several years.
adoption.koeln.politics.rec.phased.examp: What Cologne did: the project was delivered in three clearly defined phases rather than as a whole — (1) lifting the obligation to use the old cycle paths, (2) introducing 30 km/h and the first pilot stretches, (3) building out continuous 2.50 m cycle lanes. Staging it this way made it possible to evaluate each measure, build acceptance and correct course where needed, without meeting resistance head-on from the start.
adoption.koeln.politics.rec.phased.lesso: The lesson: a staged plan with clear milestones reduces conflict and builds trust. Start with cheap, quickly visible measures — marking cycle lanes, or piloting on the busiest sections. That proof-of-concept phase produces experience and a factual basis for arguing the later stages.
adoption.koeln.politics.rec.reallocation: Reallocate road space rather than build new
Cologne shows that large effects can be achieved with comparatively modest funds.

What Cologne did: the core was not costly new construction but the reallocation of existing traffic lanes — markings, signage and adjusted traffic signals. Construction costs of about €2.9 million for 9 km show that a safe cycle lane on the main network can be delivered with comparatively modest funds.

The lesson: rather than expensive new construction, cities should first examine whether lanes on busy main axes can be reallocated. That is often the fastest and cheapest route to a safe, attractive cycle network in an urban setting — and it avoids drawn-out planning and approval procedures.
adoption.koeln.politics.rec.safety.title: Clear safety standards
adoption.koeln.politics.rec.safety.claim: New cycle infrastructure stands or falls on its quality and its safety.
adoption.koeln.politics.rec.safety.examp: What Cologne did: the city set a binding standard — 2.50 m cycle lanes on the carriageway with a safety separation strip. The old side-of-the-road paths, often only 1.00 m wide, were removed accordingly. The substance of that step had broad support; the way it was carried out drew considerable public criticism, for want of transparency and communication.
adoption.koeln.politics.rec.safety.lesso: The lesson: the appeal of cycle infrastructure stands or falls on its quality and safety. Other cities should hold to minimum standards for width and visibility when planning. On main roads, cycle traffic belongs in the sight line of people driving, which minimises conflict. Turning decisively away from outdated, unsafe solutions is a central success factor.
adoption.koeln.politics.rec.structure.ti: Fit it to your own city’s structure
adoption.koeln.politics.rec.structure.cl: How far the Cologne model transfers depends heavily on the shape of the city.
adoption.koeln.politics.rec.structure.ex: What Cologne did: the project had the ring structure of the inner city to work with. That made it possible to create one continuous, easily recognised main axis for cycling — an orientation for people riding, and a clear address for political demands.
adoption.koeln.politics.rec.structure.le: The lesson: how far the Cologne model transfers depends on the shape of the city. Others should analyse their own street network and ask whether comparable main axes exist. Ideally the measure is part of a coherent overall cycling strategy — isolated measures rarely have the effect a continuous network does.

problemFit.koeln.target.11.2: The project turns old car lanes into protected bike lanes and adds eight commuter routes into the city centre, aiming to give more people convenient access to sustainable transport.
problemFit.koeln.target.11.6: By shifting car trips to bicycles, the project reduces traffic-related air pollution and noise, helping to lower the city's per-capita environmental footprint.
problemFit.koeln.intro: Cologne's bicycle network consists of two complementary components:
problemFit.koeln.ringsBody: The conversion of former car lanes on Cologne's Inner Ring into continuous 2.50-meter-wide bicycle lanes with a 30 km/h speed limit. The measure was approved by city officials in 2016 and provisionally completed in December 2024.
problemFit.koeln.routesBody: Eight radial commuter routes from the outer city districts to the city center, as well as a connecting bike ring. The network was developed in collaboration with neighboring municipalities.
problemFit.koeln.goalBody: To create a continuous, safe bicycle network that sustainably increases the share of bicycle traffic in the modal split and reduces private motorized transportation.
The project builds a continuous network of protected bike lanes and expands the Vélib' bike-sharing system across the city, aiming to give more residents (regardless of age, sex, or ability) convenient and affordable access to sustainable transport.
By shifting car trips to bicycles and calming motorized traffic, the project reduces traffic-related air pollution and noise, helping to lower the city's per-capita environmental impact.
problemFit.paris-marne-la-vallee.overvie: Paris's "Plan Vélo" is a flagship project of the city's Climate Action Plan, created to tackle the pollution, congestion, and emissions caused by decades of car-centric planning. Before the plan, a large share of trips depended on private motorized vehicles, pushing up greenhouse-gas emissions, air pollutants, and noise while cycling stayed marginal and often unsafe. Plan Vélo responds by making the bicycle a genuine primary mode of transport rather than a niche one. It works through three combined levers: infrastructure (a continuous network of protected bike lanes, many reclaimed from former car lanes, plus secure bike parking), traffic calming (lower speed limits and restrictions on through-traffic that take road space back from cars), and the expansion of public bike services such as the Vélib' bike-sharing system. Together these measures aim to give residents across the whole city safe, convenient, and affordable access to sustainable mobility. By moving journeys off cars and onto bikes, the project cuts emissions and pollution at the source and now serves as an internationally cited model for sustainable urban mobility.

impact.info.modalSplit: The modal split is the share of trips made by each mode of transport by people registered as living in Cologne.
impact.info.car: Car density is the number of registered private cars per 1,000 residents.
impact.detail.car: The figures come from the City of Cologne’s vehicle registration register (as at 31 December each year), combined with the resident population statistics.
impact.info.cycleNetwork: A distinction is drawn between the “green network” (mixed traffic on 30 km/h streets, traffic-calmed areas, cycle streets, pedestrian zones open to cycling, advisory cycle lanes or cycle paths through green space), the “yellow network” (separated from motor traffic along main roads, with cycle lanes, advisory lanes or kerbed cycle tracks) and off-street connections (away from the road space).
impact.detail.cycleNetwork: Cologne’s cycle network is maintained by the Office for Sustainable Mobility Development and published as an open geodata set. The lengths shown here are taken from that data set (as at November 2025).
impact.info.airQuality: From 2030 the EU limits tighten sharply: NO₂ from 40 to 20 µg/m³, PM10 from 40 to 20 µg/m³ and PM2.5 from 25 to 10 µg/m³, moving towards the WHO recommendations by 2050. Reducing motor traffic further is therefore decisive if those new targets are to be met.
impact.detail.airQuality: Air quality data is collected by the State Agency for Nature, Environment and Consumer Protection (LANUV) at several measuring stations in Cologne. The values shown here are annual means from the roadside station Turiner Straße (VKTU), a six-lane main road with dense building on both sides. They give the average exposure across the whole year and are the central indicator for judging compliance with the EU limits. LANUV publishes them in its annual air quality reports.
impact.info.cyclists: The city operates a network of 23 permanent automatic counting stations across Cologne. The “daily average” is the average per counting station per day — the year’s total divided by the number of days and by the number of stations. It evens out differences between locations and across the seasons, and so allows a reliable comparison from year to year.
impact.detail.cyclists: The city operates a network of 23 permanent automatic counting stations across Cologne. The “daily average” is the average per counting station per day — the year’s total divided by the number of days and by the number of stations. It evens out differences between locations and across the seasons, and so allows a reliable comparison from year to year.
impact.detail.modalSplit: The figures come from representative household surveys (MiD 2017 and the municipal mobility survey 2022, each covering mid-week working days, Tuesday to Thursday). Note that the total volume of traffic — the number of trips — rose over the period. Car traffic may therefore have grown even as its share of all trips fell.
adoption.funding.cef.details: The EU’s central programme for transport infrastructure. It funds building and modernising the trans-European transport networks (TEN-T) — cycle highways included, where they form part of a TEN-T corridor or cross a border.
adoption.funding.cef.quote: 30–85 % of eligible costs, depending on the type of project and the region.
adoption.funding.cef.access: Applications go through competitive calls run by the European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency (CINEA). Projects must show European added value (cross-border, or part of a TEN-T corridor). For a municipality this usually only comes into reach for large, supra-regional cycle-highway projects.
adoption.funding.interreg.details: Funds cross-border cooperation between European regions. Well suited to cycle networks and shared mobility plans that span cities or countries. The money comes from ERDF funds.
adoption.funding.interreg.quote: Varies by programme region; usually 60–85 % of eligible costs.
adoption.funding.interreg.access: Applications go through the individual Interreg programme regions (for example Interreg Deutschland-Nederland). A project needs partners from at least two countries. The first port of call is the Regional Coordination Office responsible for the city. The procedure is cooperative — an idea has to be agreed with that office before a formal application.
adoption.funding.erdf.details: The EU’s main instrument for regional infrastructure projects. It can be used for building cycle paths, mobility hubs and sustainable urban development.
adoption.funding.erdf.quote: Grants of up to 90 % of eligible expenditure, depending on the type and scale of the measure.
adoption.funding.erdf.access: Delivered through the federal states. In North Rhine-Westphalia the ERDF is awarded under the ERDF/JTF framework directive, and applications go to the responsible state authority (in NRW, the district governments or NRW.Bank). For many measures the NRW deadline is 30 September 2026.
adoption.funding.life.details: The EU’s environment and climate instrument. It funds climate-adaptation measures in cities — green infrastructure, biodiversity and sustainable mobility.
adoption.funding.life.quote: Usually 60 %; up to 75 % under the “Nature and Biodiversity” strand and up to 95 % under the “Clean Energy Transition” strand.
adoption.funding.life.access: Applications go through competitive CINEA calls. The German LIFE national contact point (at ZUG gGmbH) advises applicants. Projects must show a clear environmental or climate benefit, so cycling projects qualify above all where they are combined with planting, climate adaptation or biodiversity.
adoption.funding.horizon.details: Funds research and innovation across every field, mobility research included. For cycling, the relevant calls are those on sustainable urban mobility, innovative transport concepts and climate-neutral cities.
adoption.funding.horizon.quote: Usually up to 100 % of eligible project costs; the exact rate depends on the call.
adoption.funding.horizon.access: Applications go through competitive CINEA calls. Projects must be innovative and often research- or pilot-led. The entry barrier for a municipality is high, since consortia of several partners — research institutes, companies, other municipalities — are normally required. The national contact point advises applicants.
adoption.funding.ktf.details: Since 2025/2026 the central pillar of federal funding for cycling and walking. The money is bundled through the KTF and secured until 2030.
adoption.funding.ktf.access: The money flows from the federal government to the states and from there to municipalities, so applications are made to the state (in NRW, through FöRi-Nah). Applying to the federal government directly is not normally possible for infrastructure alone — the exception is funding for active mobility (non-investment model projects).
adoption.funding.kommunalrichtlinie.deta: The National Climate Initiative’s central funding instrument for municipalities. It funds investment in climate protection, cycling explicitly among it: new cycle paths, cycle lanes, cycle streets, junctions, cycle parking and bike-and-ride. Cycle highways are not eligible.
adoption.funding.kommunalrichtlinie.quot: Up to 50 % of eligible costs; up to 65 % for municipalities in financial difficulty.
adoption.funding.kommunalrichtlinie.acce: Applications go to the project agency Zukunft-Umwelt-Gesellschaft (ZUG) gGmbH, and can be submitted again from 1 February 2025. Funding is competitive. Projects up to €6 million are approved as fixed-sum financing.
adoption.funding.bundesstrassen.details: These measures are not funded but financed in full by the federal government, because federal roads are its responsibility. The money comes from the federal budget rather than the KTF.
adoption.funding.bundesstrassen.access: Not a funding programme for municipalities but a federal task. Planning and delivery sit with the federal government (its road construction administration). Municipalities can, however, register needs and take part in the planning.
adoption.info.timeline: The timeline runs from the citizens’ initiative to the last gap closed — and what is still outstanding.
adoption.info.cost: Covers the construction costs alone — markings, signage, spot resurfacing and removing the old cycle paths. Not a total budget, and it refers to the sections delivered up to May 2023.
adoption.detail.cost: The figure was announced at a joint press conference of the City of Cologne and the Kölner Stadt-Anzeiger on 15 May 2023. Renewing the traffic signals (€1.5 million) was due anyway and is not included. No separate figures were published for the planning and consultancy costs, for the gaps closed in 2024, or for the Ebertplatz redesign still to come.
adoption.info.context: Cologne is Germany’s fourth-largest city, with a population density typical of large European cities. The inner ring — a main road running along the line of the medieval city wall — was fitted with continuous cycle lanes between 2018 and 2024, over some 10 km, five in each direction.
